title: The Prism Lab
summary: Find a prism’s sweet spot of least bend, retune it in a gel chamber and keep a photon bouncing in a game of light Pong.
subject: physics
concepts: Total internal reflection in a prism
learningOutcome: The student can find n = sin((A + D)/2)/sin(A/2) from the minimum deviation, shift it for a prism in a liquid, and find the incidence at which a ray is just totally reflected at the second face.

levels.title: The sweet spot
levels.adds: Baseline: the bend is least when the ray crosses the prism symmetrically, and n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2) follows from it (Ex 9.6).
hints: Two incidence angles that bend the beam by the same amount lie either side of the sweet spot, and it is near the middle of them.
At the least bend the ray inside makes A/2 with each normal, and i = (A + D)/2.
n = sin i / sin(A/2), with the angle of least bend D read from your test beams.

levels.title: The gel chamber
levels.adds: New idea: in a gel the prism acts like glass of index n/n(gel), so the sweet spot moves to sin i = (n/n_gel) sin(A/2) (Ex 9.6, prism in water).
hints: Replace n by the relative index n(glass)/n(gel).
At the least bend the ray inside still makes A/2 with the normals.
sin i = (n/n_gel) × sin(A/2). Use the inverse sine in degrees.

levels.title: Photon Pong
levels.adds: New idea: Photon is just totally reflected at the second face when r₂ equals the critical angle, which fixes the widest entry angle (Ex 9.21).
hints: r₁ + r₂ = A. The ray bounces back off the second face when r₂ is at least the critical angle c, with sin c = 1/n.
The widest entry angle has r₁ = A − c.
Then sin i = n sin r₁.

misconceptions: The prism bends light least when it enters along the normal
A prism bends light just as much in water as in air
Total internal reflection depends on the angle at the first face only
